Sizing
  • 1 unit = 1.00u (0.9% of the roll, reset monthly up or down).
  • Normal play: 1u. LEAN (unproven model): 0u. Great play: up to 3u, only for a PLAY, sized by ¼-Kelly.
  • Never more than 4u on one game, the same leg in more than 2 entries, or 15% of the roll open at once.

Discipline

1 bet(s) above the 3-unit cap, 0 stake increase(s) straight after a loss. The system's real failure mode is not a losing run, it is what gets bet after one.

Calibration

When a bet was logged at X%, did it win X%? The gap is only real if this holds.

No settled bets with a recorded estimate yet. Once bets grade, this answers the question the whole system rests on: when you say 70%, does it win 70%?

House rules

  • One unit per bet. Not two because you love it.
  • A bet needs a positive gap, not a big favourite. High probability is not an edge.
  • If nothing clears the bar, bet nothing. A no-bet day is a normal day.
  • Three losses in a row does not change tomorrow's unit.
  • The unit moves once a month, on the bankroll, never on a feeling.
  • Write the reason and the biggest risk before the result is known.
  • No parlays as strategy. Correlated legs are one bet, not several.
  • Don't chase a price that has already moved.

Bets

Log it

After a bet settles: what is in the app, what is still riding, and how much to take out. Nothing you type here is saved or published.

Saves to your private betting repo on GitHub (you must be signed in); the Mac picks it up within about 5 minutes and this page updates.
Logging a bet
  • Tell Claude what you placed ("1u Allen under 36.5 rush at -105 on DK") and it logs it.
  • Or yourself: edge hq bet "BUF@LA" "Josh Allen U36.5 rush" --price -105 --units 1 --book dk
  • Settle a prop or pick'em: edge hq settle <bet id> win (spreads/totals grade themselves with edge grade).

What the history says

  • College: each extra point of spread changes the dog's cover rate at spread ÷ 4 by -0.40 points (z -6.9), so a wider spread hurts the dog; Power vs Power -0.43 (z -4.4). Power-vs-Power dogs of 14-20.5 covered 49.0% (678 games) and 21-30.5 48.5% (374), against 52.4% needed at -110.
  • NFL: -0.83 points per point of spread (z -3.7), so a wider spread hurts the dog.
  • Dogs win the 1st vs the game. College 14-20.5 point dogs win the 1st 20% vs the game 12%; NFL 10-13.5 point dogs 26% vs 16%.
  • Home vs road dog is shown in the Venue filter: college home dogs' spread trend -0.48/pt (z -3.9), road dogs -0.35/pt (z -5.0).
  • All of this assumes the 1st-quarter line really is spread ÷ 4. Where a book posts that line, the table is the answer; use the Lines at spread ÷ 4 table for the price. Kalshi lists several 1Q lines per game, and the cards above compare its actual prices with the same history.

Paper only: these prices know the pregame spread and nothing else (no injuries, weather or team news) and have not yet been graded against real results, so the system stakes 0 units on them. Kalshi limit orders on 1st-quarter markets must expire at kickoff, because these markets keep trading during the game.

What the history says

  • College: each extra point of spread changes the dog's cover rate at spread ÷ 4 by -0.39 points (z -6.6), so a wider spread hurts the dog; Power vs Power -0.40 (z -4.1). Power-vs-Power dogs of 14-20.5 covered 47.9% (678 games) and 21-30.5 42.7% (374), against 52.4% needed at -110.
  • NFL: -0.75 points per point of spread (z -3.3), so a wider spread hurts the dog.
  • Dogs win the 2nd vs the game. College 14-20.5 point dogs win the 2nd 23% vs the game 12%; NFL 10-13.5 point dogs 27% vs 16%.
  • Home vs road dog is shown in the Venue filter: college home dogs' spread trend -0.29/pt (z -2.3), road dogs -0.42/pt (z -5.9).
  • All of this assumes the 2nd-quarter line really is spread ÷ 4. Where a book posts that line, the table is the answer; use the Lines at spread ÷ 4 table for the price. Kalshi lists several 2Q lines per game, and the cards above compare its actual prices with the same history.

Paper only: these prices know the pregame spread and nothing else (no injuries, weather or team news) and have not yet been graded against real results, so the system stakes 0 units on them. Kalshi limit orders on 2nd-quarter markets must expire at kickoff, because these markets keep trading during the game.

  • College: each extra point of spread changes the dog's cover rate at spread ÷ 4 by -0.30 points (z -5.2), so a wider spread hurts the dog; Power vs Power -0.22 (z -2.2). Power-vs-Power dogs of 14-20.5 covered 47.7% (678 games) and 21-30.5 49.1% (374), against 52.4% needed at -110.
  • NFL: -0.79 points per point of spread (z -3.5), so a wider spread hurts the dog.
  • Dogs win the 3rd vs the game. College 14-20.5 point dogs win the 3rd 21% vs the game 12%; NFL 10-13.5 point dogs 25% vs 16%.
  • Home vs road dog is shown in the Venue filter: college home dogs' spread trend -0.41/pt (z -3.3), road dogs -0.30/pt (z -4.3).
  • All of this assumes the 3rd-quarter line really is spread ÷ 4. Where a book posts that line, the table is the answer; use the Lines at spread ÷ 4 table for the price. Kalshi lists several 3Q lines per game, and the cards above compare its actual prices with the same history.

Paper only: these prices know the pregame spread and nothing else (no injuries, weather or team news) and have not yet been graded against real results, so the system stakes 0 units on them. Kalshi limit orders on 3rd-quarter markets must expire at kickoff, because these markets keep trading during the game.

The study: do dogs beat a 4th-quarter line of spread ÷ 4?

Every game since 2011 (NFL) and 2014 (college), closing spreads, 4th quarter only (overtime excluded). "Covers ÷4 line" assumes the 4th-quarter line is exactly the pregame spread ÷ 4; at -110 it needs 52.4% to profit (green = the whole 95% range is above that). "4th minus game" = how much more often the dog wins the 4th quarter than it wins the game, in points.

Do bigger spreads help the dog?

Favourites coast: they win the 4th by much less than spread ÷ 4 at every size. But they still win it, and by more points as the spread grows, so at the lines Kalshi posts (+1.5 to +3.5) a wider spread is worse for the dog. Wide-spread dogs pay only at bigger lines (+6.5, +7.5) bought under the cheat-sheet price. Uses the College / NFL switch above.

What the history says

  • College: a wider spread helps the dog cover spread ÷ 4. +0.28 points of cover rate per point of spread (z +4.8); Power vs Power +0.34 (z +3.5). Power-vs-Power dogs of 14-20.5 covered 58.0% (678 games) and 21-30.5 57.6% (374), against 52.4% needed at -110.
  • NFL: the opposite. -0.56 points per point of spread (z -2.5); big NFL dogs cover less. Look at small and mid NFL spreads.
  • Dogs win the 4th far more often than they win the game. College 14-20.5 point dogs win the 4th 25% vs the game 12%; NFL 10-13.5 point dogs 33% vs 16%.
  • Home vs road dog is shown in the Venue filter: college home dogs' spread trend +0.12/pt (z +1.0), road dogs +0.34/pt (z +4.8).
  • All of this assumes the 4th-quarter line really is spread ÷ 4. Where a book posts that line, the table is the answer; use the Lines at spread ÷ 4 table for the price. Kalshi lists several 4Q lines per game, and the cards above compare its actual prices with the same history.

Paper only: these prices know the pregame spread and nothing else (no injuries, weather or team news) and have not yet been graded against real results, so the system stakes 0 units on them. Kalshi limit orders on 4th-quarter markets must expire at kickoff, because these markets keep trading during the game.

Your entries vs the average entry

Splash's "est. value" treats every alive entry the same: prize ÷ entries alive. The model prices each entry on the teams it has LEFT against the teams every other alive entry has left (best remaining path, over the weeks the pool is likely to last), so an entry holding teams the field has burned is worth more, and one that burned teams the field still holds is worth less. "Of your path" = how much of the entry's survival odds that team carries (or would add back). Buyers pay the same multiple for strong and weak entries, so the strongest are the ones to keep.

How to read it: each row is a team’s remaining season, one cell per leg, numbers are its win probability there (horizon-widened — a December cell is a forecast of a line, not a line). Future value adds up how much better than a coin flip those spots are (only the part above 60% counts, because a 55% spot is not a survivor pick) — it is the same number the field model and the champion model use, and the teams at the top are the ones you want to still be holding in December. Cost to burn is what taking the team this week knocks off your best remaining path — the board’s “Future cost” column, shown here beside the schedule it comes from. The brightest cell in a row is the best spot the team has left. Holiday spots matter out of proportion: none left are a separate contest week with a short team list, and running out of eligible teams for one is the most common way a live entry actually dies. Free for = how many of your entries have not spent the team yet.

How teams move during a season

How much teams move: a team's rating shifts by ±2.7 points (sd) between September and December; the traits above explain 5% of that, so most of it is unforeseeable — which is why every future leg's spread is widened by 0.32 pts per week of lookahead, calibrated to that number, and why the whole map re-prices every 2 hours as the market learns. The predictable part is applied at 50% strength, ramping in over the season.
Biggest expected movers this year: MIA +0.5, BUF -0.5, JAX -0.4, ARI +0.4, NYJ +0.4, LA -0.3, KC -0.3, HOU -0.3.

How past Circa champions played it

Leg-by-leg analysis of the 480 champion picks: average pick 75% to win; the #1 favourite only 31% of the time (top-2 48%, top-3 59%); their pick carried 27% of the field on average while the chalk carried 41%; only 5% of picks were under 60% to win. Chalk rate by season phase: 38% (legs 1–6), 40% (7–12), 17% (13+). Holiday legs: average 64% to win. Champions who owned several entries split them in 83% of legs where two or more were alive — and the extra entries went a rung or two down: average 72% to win (vs 80% for the primary), median #4 favourite, 38% of the time 10+ points below the primary, and a third of them on bottom-half future-value teams (e.g. 2025 Week 1: DEN on the main entry, ARI / JAX / PIT on the others).

What a champion would do this week

A choice model fitted on all 480 champion picks (with each champion's remaining teams and the field's actual pick share that leg) says a champion in your seat picks: LA 58%, BUF 16%, SEA 11%, BAL 7%, SF 2%. With 1 entries that becomes LA. What the fit learned: champions treat a 75% and a 90% favourite almost alike, avoid burning teams with future value, prefer home teams, do not shy from Thursday games, and lean with the field when its share is high — their edge came from the paths they kept, not from fading chalk for its own sake.

Gold rows are teams the model suggests for one of your entries. Range is the 10th–90th percentile this projection has landed in out of sample — the grey block on the bar. Public pools is SurvivorGrid’s Yahoo/ESPN consensus, usually more lopsided than the model’s projection. Still have it is the share of alive entries that have not spent the team yet; a team most of the field has burned cannot be popular however good the spot is. Leverage is how much bigger your share of the pot gets if you take the team and it wins.

Tested by holding each season out of the fit and projecting it blind (53 legs with 500+ entries, 2021–2026): the model names the field’s most popular team 64% of the time and is off by 12% of pick share on it, and 21% of the field’s picks land on a team other than the one predicted for them. That is the honest accuracy of the range column — it is measured, not asserted, and it is why the range is quoted at all.

Where the number comes from

A conditional-logit choice model fitted to every Circa selections PDF since 2021 (the only pick-by-pick survivor data published anywhere), projected onto this pool’s surviving entries — 109 legs, each entry’s exact remaining teams as its menu, so a team two-thirds of the field has already spent is not projected as chalk. What it reads: win probability, where the team sits on the board, what the rest of that team’s schedule is worth, holiday legs it can still cover, kickoff slot, home/away, opponent quality, and two behavioural terms — the field gets chalkier right after a bloodbath, and shifts as the pool shrinks. Source: 617 alive after W9 (the pool's count); what they used in W9 is the pool's own pick %. Field learning: temperature ×1.02 (1.00 = the 2021–25 average field; higher = chalkier), chalk bias +0.14.

What the field has already burned: KC 77%, MIN 68%, CIN 62%, SF 60%, JAX 54%, NE 54%, HOU 45%, DET 40%, BAL 35%, SEA 28%, DEN 27%, DAL 22%.

That is a sharper field than this one; how well it transfers to a public Splash field is not measured. Nothing here is re-stated after the fact.

Chalk traps ahead

The weeks where the field is projected to pile onto a team that is not actually good — it drew the crowd by drawing a bad opponent. Being somewhere else those weeks is cheap leverage: the one time in three or four the chalk loses, a big slice of the pot goes with it. Flagged: a team on 25%+ of the field that sits outside our top 10 and is playing a bottom-ten team, or any chalk under 60% to win.

How this is built. Field shares for later weeks come from rolling the pool's whole field forward through the same pick model that projects this week, so each week’s number already has the field’s earlier picks spent. The range is how far a projection that size has landed from reality this season; a projection months out is looser than that. “Our board” is the Power rankings tab. Pivots are teams that leg winning 60%+ with under 15% of the field, and never a team your entry has already used. The chalk is not expected to lose more often than its line says — the edge is that when it does, the field shrinks and you are not in the pile. The plan maximises the chance of getting through every leg, so it is often on the chalk; each card shows what a pivot costs in win probability.

Bear's $50K Survivor 2026 · looking past W10 (Week 10)

Look Ahead

A look ahead is a forecast of a forecast. Nothing on this tab is a pick, and the lines it prices do not exist yet — a future leg's number is this week's market rating widened for everything that can still happen between now and then (injuries, form, the line itself moving). Use it to see which weeks are thin, what a pick this week costs you later, and which teams to keep — not to commit. The week you are actually submitting is on This week's suggestions.
Every future leg is priced from the same market-implied ratings and Elo the rest of the site uses, widened by 0.32 points of spread per week of lookahead and tilted by each team's expected trajectory. The pool's field is rolled forward through the choice model (fitted on Circa's selections) from 617 alive after W9 (the pool's count); what they used in W9 is the pool's own pick %: 617 entries alive now, spending teams every week — 120 simulated seasons of 6,000 entries, each season sharing one outcome per game so entries on the same team live and die together. Survivor counts are projections with a few percent of simulation error around them and are shown to two figures for that reason. Your assumptions live in this browser only. Season Map

Every number re-prices on each rebuild (every 2 hours, every 5 minutes on game days): 24 of 272 games carry DraftKings' current line via ESPN (as of 2026-11-13 04:22Z); the rest use market-implied ratings re-solved from today's lines (recent weeks weighted most) blended with Elo, which moves after every result. Far-off legs are tilted by each team's expected trajectory (↑/↓ on the row) and widened for the movement history says to expect.

Every path on this map is a model suggestion, not a committed plan. The grid re-solves the best surviving route from the current numbers each time you lock a cell — it shows what the maths would do, not what has been entered on Splash. Only cells marked submitted / locked are real picks.
Under the win %, also show: Click a cell to lock that team for that leg; the rest of the season re-solves for the best surviving path. Click ✕ on a team to exclude it (injury, "never again"). Everything you set stays in this browser.
Stance: Numbered dots show which entries are on a cell. "Together" re-solves all alive entries as one portfolio under the stance (the same γ the card uses) so they do not all die on the same Sunday; your locks always win.

    Portfolio

    Entries in the config but not in Splash's standings (they are left off below): Warren Sharp's $100K: RPERLICH #1

    Portfolio play

    One pick per entry, chosen across all your pools together for the best chance of winning at least one of them. This week's games are played out jointly, so two entries on the same team win and lose together.

    Spread gives up at most 1% of the best chance to make losing every entry in one weekend as unlikely as possible. All-in is the strict maximum. At these odds your chance of winning at least one is almost exactly the sum of each entry's own chance, so the two differ by hundredths of a point; what spreading really buys is not losing everything on one upset.
